title: Agile product management after the project
blurb: Decide how a product keeps improving once the project ends: flexible roadmap, short prioritized cycles and wide collaboration.
question: After Pinewick Home and Garden's click and collect project closes, customers ask for a 'tell me when it's back in stock' feature. How should this be handled under agile product management?

teach.body: A project is temporary: it introduces a change into business as usual and then closes. The product it delivers usually lives on and keeps improving. Agile product management is the strategic and tactical way of managing that ongoing product development with agile frameworks and techniques such as Scrum and Kanban. Each release should add value, and the product is steered by feedback rather than by a fixed plan made up front.

teach.h: Key features of agile product management
head: Feature
What it means in practice
rows: A high-level vision with a flexible roadmap, adjusted from stakeholder, customer and market feedback
Short cycles (sprints or iterations); features ranked by business value, user feedback and market needs
Product managers work closely with development, design and other stakeholders
Customer feedback gathered continually; iterative planning and adaptation so each release adds value

teach.caption: Feedback from customers, stakeholders and the market reshapes the roadmap continually.

rows.label: Life span
values: Ongoing while the product is used

items.label: E-commerce team improves the service in sprints

teach.h: Worked scenario: Pinewick Home and Garden's click and collect
teach.body: After closure, the e-commerce team keeps improving click and collect as normal business, and the stores run collection every day. Marcus Lindell, head of e-commerce, keeps a high-level vision ('the easiest way to get garden goods today') and a roadmap he revises as feedback arrives. A 'back in stock' alert goes into the backlog and is ranked against locker improvements by value and customer feedback. Store managers, designers and developers review each release together.

teach.text: Traps: starting a new project for each enhancement goes against agile product management. The roadmap is flexible, not fixed for years. Collaboration is wide (development, design, stakeholders), not limited to one owner, and ownership is shared rather than centrally controlled.

items: Agile product management: ongoing product development with frameworks such as Scrum and Kanban.
High-level vision plus a flexible roadmap, adjusted from feedback.
Short cycles, prioritized by business value, user feedback and market needs.
Close collaboration with development, design and stakeholders.
Enhancements go through product iterations, not a new project each time.

summary: You can now apply agile product management to a product once its project has closed. You can keep a vision and a flexible roadmap, prioritize short cycles by value and feedback, and route enhancements through product iterations rather than new projects.

A.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's click and collect project has closed and the e-commerce team now improves the service as normal business. Customers ask for an alert when an out-of-stock item returns to their store. Which action BEST applies agile product management?
options: Start a new PRINCE2 Agile project with its own canvas
Hold the idea until the annual roadmap review
Ask the former project board to approve the change
Add it to the backlog, ranked by value and feedback
A.why: Agile product management handles enhancements in short cycles, prioritizing features by business value, user feedback and market needs (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.0: Starting a new project for each enhancement is not how agile product management delivers improvements to a live product.
whyNot.1: Waiting for an annual review replaces continual adjustment with a fixed cycle.
whyNot.2: The project board ceased with the project; the live product is steered through product prioritization.

A.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's Smart Maintenance project has closed. Ruth Kenyon's maintenance team owns the dashboard and the software team keeps improving it. How should the dashboard's future direction be managed?
options: Through a high-level vision and a feedback-led roadmap
Through a detailed feature list fixed for the next two years
Through a yearly release containing all agreed improvements
Through the software team lead's plan, set apart from engineers
A.why: Agile product managers keep a high-level product vision and align work to it through a flexible roadmap that is continually adjusted from stakeholder, customer and market feedback (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.1: A fixed two-year feature list removes the flexibility the roadmap needs.
whyNot.2: One yearly release abandons short cycles and frequent feedback.
whyNot.3: Agile product management depends on close collaboration with stakeholders and users.

A.q: Callowmere University's Student Support Hub is live and the web team improves it in two-week sprints. Student feedback shows that the booking screen confuses screen reader users, so the product manager moves a fix to the top of the next sprint. Which feature of agile product management is being applied?
options: Product vision and roadmap
Iteration and prioritization
Collaboration with teams
Transition to operations
A.why: Iteration and prioritization means short cycles in which features and improvements are ranked by business value, user feedback and changing needs (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.0: The vision and roadmap set direction; reordering the next sprint from feedback is prioritization.
whyNot.2: Collaboration is about working closely with development, design and stakeholders, not ranking the next sprint.
whyNot.3: Transition to operations is the hand-over at the end of the project, not ongoing prioritization.

B.q: After Easterholm County Council's Care Online project closes, Helen Crowther proposes that the digital team decides all future features by itself, with no input from social care operations staff or the carers' network. Which approach would BETTER apply agile product management?
options: Let the cabinet approve every change in advance
Freeze features until a new project is approved
Ask Abacus to set the priorities for the service
Work with practitioners, carers and designers
B.why: Agile product managers work closely with development, design and other stakeholders so the product meets both business objectives and user needs (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.0: Advance approval of every change slows short cycles and is not how agile product management steers a product.
whyNot.1: Freezing features until a new project starts replaces ongoing iterations with a project per change.
whyNot.2: A supplier setting priorities would not reflect user needs and business value.

B.q: Larkspur Rail's Fair Fares project has closed. Matteo Ricci, head of digital products, now plans how the app will evolve over the coming year, including ideas for showing passengers their carbon savings. Which approach is MOST in line with agile product management?
options: Fix next year's features now so the budget is certain
Run each new idea as its own short PRINCE2 Agile project
Keep a vision and adjust the roadmap from user feedback
Collect all ideas and build them in one large release
B.why: A high-level product vision guides a flexible roadmap that is continually adjusted from stakeholder, customer and market feedback (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.0: Fixing a year of features up front removes the roadmap's flexibility.
whyNot.1: Enhancements to a live product are handled in product iterations, not separate projects.
whyNot.3: One large release delays feedback; each release should add value incrementally.

B.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's digital team continues to improve the tenant portal after the project closes. Which statement BEST describes how its work differs from the project's?
options: It runs in stages approved by a board with tolerances
It continues in short cycles steered by feedback
It follows the closed project's release map to the end
It waits for a mandate before each improvement
B.why: Agile product management manages the product lifecycle through short, prioritized cycles of planning, feedback and adaptation, so each release adds value (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.0: Stages, a board and tolerances describe the project's governance, not ongoing product work.
whyNot.2: The release map belonged to the project; the product is steered by a flexible roadmap.
whyNot.3: A mandate triggers a project; ongoing improvements go through product iterations.

C.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's click and collect service is live. Marcus Lindell proposes that every future improvement, such as extra lockers or faster collection slots, is run as a separate PRINCE2 Agile project with its own board. Is this an appropriate application of agile product management, and why?
options: Yes, because PRINCE2 Agile is designed for projects
Yes, because each change needs its own business case
No, because enhancements run in product iterations
No, because live services stop being prioritized
C.why: Enhancements after a project are handled through agile product management iterations, prioritized by value and feedback, not by starting a new project for each one (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.0: PRINCE2 Agile is for projects, but that does not mean every enhancement to a live product needs one.
whyNot.1: Ongoing improvements are prioritized by value within product management, not justified one by one as projects.
whyNot.3: The verdict is right but the reason is wrong: live products are prioritized continually.

C.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's dashboard is live. Its product manager fixes the feature roadmap for the next 18 months and declines engineers' requests to change it, to keep the plan stable. Is this an appropriate application of agile product management, and why?
options: Yes, because a stable plan protects machine availability
Yes, because the project's release map has been closed
No, because the roadmap needs the board's approval
No, because the roadmap should adapt to feedback
C.why: The roadmap is flexible and continually adjusted from stakeholder, customer and market feedback (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.0: Availability depends on a useful product; refusing feedback does not protect it.
whyNot.1: The release map has closed with the project, but that is no reason to fix the product roadmap.
whyNot.2: The verdict is right but the reason is wrong: the project board does not steer the live product.

C.q: Callowmere University's hub is live. Rebecca Lyle ranks improvements every two weeks by value and student feedback, and wellbeing staff and the students' union review each release with the team. Is this an appropriate application of agile product management, and why?
options: Yes, because it prioritizes short cycles with stakeholders
Yes, because the release map now replaces the product roadmap
No, because improvements need a new project mandate
No, because sprints end when the project has closed
C.why: Agile product management uses short, prioritized cycles and close collaboration with stakeholders so each release adds value (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.1: The release map was the project's plan; the product is steered by a flexible roadmap.
whyNot.2: Enhancements to a live product run in product iterations; a new mandate is not needed.
whyNot.3: Short cycles continue in product management after the project closes.

reteach.title: Running a popular café after opening
reteach.question: Once a new café has opened, how does the owner decide what to change on the menu?

blocks.h: Opening is a project; running is a product
blocks.body: Opening the café was a project with a deadline. Now the owner keeps a clear idea of what the café stands for, tries a new dish each week, listens to customers and staff, and drops what does not sell. Nobody sets up a new project to add a soup. The menu plan changes as the owner learns.

head: Café
Product management
rows: Menu plan revised as you learn
A new dish each week, best sellers first
Chef, staff and regulars agree changes

blocks.text: Printing a menu that cannot change for two years, or hiring a project team for each new dish, both miss the point.

explain.body: It is the strategic and tactical approach to managing product development with agile frameworks and techniques, such as Scrum and Kanban, through iterative planning, feedback and adaptation.

test.q: Easterholm County Council's digital team will keep improving Care Online after the project. Which description of agile product management should it follow?
options: Managing the product with fixed annual plans and sign-offs
Managing the product through agile frameworks and feedback
Managing the product as a chain of short separate projects
Managing the product through the supplier's release cycle
test.why: Agile product management manages product development with agile frameworks and techniques such as Scrum and Kanban, through iterative planning, feedback and adaptation (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.0: Fixed annual plans remove the iterative planning and adaptation it depends on.
whyNot.2: Enhancements are delivered in product iterations, not as a chain of projects.
whyNot.3: A supplier's cycle does not set the product's priorities or vision.

explain.body: The product manager keeps a high-level vision and aligns the team to it through a roadmap that is continually adjusted from stakeholder, customer and market feedback.

test.q: Larkspur Rail's passenger panel reports that delay alerts arrive too late to be useful. How should the app's roadmap respond under agile product management?
options: Adjust the roadmap to reflect the panel's feedback
Keep the roadmap until the next annual planning round
Raise a request for change to the closed project board
Add the feedback to the lessons report for future projects
test.why: The roadmap is continually adjusted based on feedback from stakeholders, customers and market conditions (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.1: Waiting for an annual round removes the flexibility the roadmap needs.
whyNot.2: A closed project's board no longer controls the live product.
whyNot.3: The lessons report helps future projects; it does not steer the live product's roadmap.

explain.body: Agile product managers work closely with development, design and other stakeholders so the product aligns with business objectives and user needs. Ownership is shared, not centrally controlled.

test.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's portal is live. When the digital team decides what to improve next, who should it work with MOST closely under agile product management?
options: Tenants, repairs staff, designers and developers
The former project board, which approves each idea
The chief executive, who sets each sprint's content
Coastline's managers, who rank the portal backlog
test.why: Agile product management depends on close collaboration with development, design and other stakeholders so the product meets business objectives and user needs (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.1: The project board ended with the project; it does not approve live product changes.
whyNot.2: Central control of each sprint's content runs against shared ownership and team prioritization.
whyNot.3: A supplier ranking the backlog would not balance tenants' needs and business value.

explain.body: Once a product is live, enhancements are prioritized and delivered in product management iterations. Starting a new project for each one is not the agile product management approach.

test.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's engineers ask for a new chart on the live dashboard. Which route BEST fits agile product management?
options: A new project with its own mandate, canvas and board
A formal change request to the original project board
A backlog entry, ranked for a coming iteration
A note in the closed project's lessons log for later
test.why: Enhancements to a live product are handled in product management iterations, prioritized by value and feedback (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.0: A new project per enhancement is not how a live product is improved.
whyNot.1: The original project board no longer governs the live product.
whyNot.3: A lessons log records lessons; it does not deliver product improvements.
